recipes.name: No-Knead Bread
ingredients_raw: 1.6666667461395 cups warm water (110 degrees F/45 degrees C)

steps.text: Combine the flour, yeast, and salt in a large bowl and mix to combine. Add water and herbs, if using, and mix well. The dough will be very sticky and shaggy-looking. Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and set aside at room temperature for 18 to 24 hours.

Generously flour a work surface. The dough will have risen and will be covered in bubbles. Transfer the dough to the work surface and dust it with flour. Fold the dough in half, and then form the dough into a ball by stretching and tucking the edges of the dough underneath the ball.
Liberally flour a kitchen towel (do not use terrycloth). Place the dough ball on the floured towel. Cover with another floured towel. Let the dough rise for about two hours [see footnote].
Preheat the oven to 450 degrees F (230 degrees C). Place a lidded Dutch oven or deep heavy duty casserole dish (with lid) into the oven to preheat.
Carefully remove the hot baking dish from the oven. Remove the lid and gently turn the dough ball into the ungreased baking dish, seam-side up; shake the dish so the dough is more evenly distributed.
Cover and bake for 30 minutes. Remove the lid and bake until the crust is golden brown, 15 to 20 minutes. Remove the loaf from the baking dish and let it cool on a rack before slicing.

raw_recipe.headline: No-Knead Bread
raw_recipe.description: This no knead bread is as easy to make as it sounds — no kneading, fancy equipment, or effort needed to get a crusty artisan loaf just like you’d get at a bakery.

video.description: No need to be intimidated by a beautiful loaf of bread . . . you can achieve a great crumb and gorgeous crust with very little effort—just bake in your heavy casserole dish or Dutch oven. Simply mix all of the ingredients: flour, yeast, salt, warm water and herbs, if you like—rosemary, thyme, sage. Then allow for the dough to develop overnight, form into a ball and allow to rise for a couple of hours and bake in a preheated dish covered, then uncovered to achieve the golden crust. Cool, cut and serve with plenty of butter!

review.reviewBody: I've been baking no-knead bread ever since the original recipe came out in the New York Times several years ago, so trust me when I tell you it is not recommended that you remove the baking vessel from the oven after you've just spent 30 minutes heating it. Do NOT remove it from the oven, just pour the dough (batter, really) into the baking vessel and then cover and bake. That way you don't lose the heat you just spent half an hour to achieve to heat the pan. Also, there's no need to shake the dough once it's in the pan, it'll spread by itself while baking. It's really a misnomer to call this a dough, because it really comes out as a batter. I agree with the other reviewer that it's impossible to form it into any kind of a ball 'cause it's just too sticky. And forget the step of placing it on a towel to raise. It's just messy and doesn't achieve anything more than if you just stir it and place it in a bowl and let it rise another 2 hours. That said, I would rate this a 4, only because I think the instructions are not the best way to make this bread.

I became an avid bread maker when I discovered Jim Lahey's recipe. I wanted to post it, but you beat me to it, Jewissa. I'll have to try adding the fresh herbs, though. Great idea! Proud as a peacock, I brought a few slices from my first loaf to work. One of my colleagues, who lived many years in various European countries, picked up a piece and immediately identified it as European peasant bread. After one bite, she said, "I need this recipe." (She hasn't bothered with recipes in years!) BTW, the "heavy-duty casserole dish" should be either cast iron or stoneware. I've read that Le Creuset works fine, as long as you remove the handles, which aren't oven-safe at 450 F. UPDATE: I brought this bread (minus the herbs) to a staff potluck, and it was a great success. There were many recipe requests. Those who've tried it are converts. The only challenges are to find the proper pot and to figure out the timing. I haven't bought bread since I discovered this recipe!
2ND UPDATE: I've found, tweeked, and posted a recipe for a healthier yet delicious whole-wheat multi-grain bread which uses the same method.

I followed the recipe all the way except for the herbs, just added a touch of rosemary for the first one. Also, I placed the dough on a piece of parchment before putting it in the dutch oven. DELICIOUS bread!!! I made another one today! One other note...I used bread flour instead of AP.

I love this recipe. I found a product I had not seen before, Platinum Instant Sourdough Yeast + Sourdough Culture, and used it. It turned out great! I will say that the dough was so wet after the first rise that I added about another 1/2 cup of flour while trying to get it to a manageable ball. Once I got it to the point I could pick it up, I did the towel thing and when it was ready, put it on a piece of parchment and dumped the whole thing in my Lodge cast iron pan. I am surprised at the tang and the 'sourdoughness' of the end product! Will definitely use this recipe and the sourdough yeast again.

A few tips for making the dough: First thing, measure 375ml of very hot water, then add 2 tsp of coarse salt - it will dissolve while you measure the flour. I use a food scale to weigh out exactly 450 g of bread flour. Add the dry yeast into the flour and mix completely. Then add the hot water, about 1/3 each time and mix with a (hand-held) dough whisk until just mixed. Proceed with recipe as written. Note: if you refrigerated the dough overnight, transfer to a different bowl for the final rise so the dough reaches room temp faster.

I've been experimenting with all sorts of bread recipes this summer. this one's a total winner, came out exactly as described. I added some rosemary and dill, did second rise in a floured bowl in unlit oven with hot water underneath. used mixer to mix initial ingredients and dough hook very briefly
to make the ball. sprinkled cornmeal bottom of Dutch oven so no sticking.

I made this recipe that is very close to the new York times recipe.
What happened to me when making the NYT recipe is that my oven cut out( breaker?) after 30 minutes. I just left the loaf covered for another 25-30 minutes . Turned out GREAT.
So I did the same with this one. 450 F for 30 mins then turned the oven off and left loaf COVERED for another 25-30 minutes.
What you have is an amazing crust..
Try it.
portions of water flour yeast ect is way better in this recipe
I did cut salt by half and it was perfect for my taste buds

I proofed the yeast first for five minutes then allowed the dough to rise for about 6 hours. I kneaded a little and allowed it to rise again in the oven on a proof setting for an hour. Then baked according to the recipe. Came out amazing! Use the Dutch oven! It creates a PERFECT crust!

This is the second time I made this bread in two weeks. It is so good! This time I decided to skip the towel and flour bit and just put it in a bread pan to rise and bake. Much simpler and came out perfectly!

I use this recipe both as a no-knead and kneaded dough recipe. I recommend using more like 3 and 1/2 to almost 4 cups of flour (I use bread flour). I also reduced the heat of the oven to 425 degrees because of the parchment paper I use to bake and the bread came out with a softer, easier to chew and cut, crust. I baked it for about 35 minutes (20 minutes with the lid on the dutch oven, and 15 minutes without). This is my go to recipe.
This came out great!!!!
I'm adding garlic, Parmesan and some shredded cheese to finally dough before baking..
Hit the dough with a light mist of water and put Parmesan and rosemary on top after scoring it.

The ingredients in this recipe are way off. For 3 cups of flour, 2 teaspoons of salt is FAR too much and will result in bread too salty to enjoy. 1 to 1 1/4 teaspoons of salt is the right amount. And 1 2/3 cups of water is too much. The resulting dough will be too moist and sticky and you won't be able to manipulate it into a ball. 1 1/3 cups water is the correct amount. It should require some effort to get the water mixed into the flour/salt/yeast.

Much like some other Breads made “without” using a (BIGGA). By adding Bagga one gets a More rustic sourdough (type) flavor. Baked @450 some 50 min. Top off with Aprox 15/20 to finish . This was a Aprox 1200 gram loaf.
Good recipe, but use less water. I do 1 1/2 cups. If you want a dough that is an actual ball and not flat, use less water. It makes my bread loaves more like loaves instead of disks.

Easy to follow recipe, let it proof for 24 hours, it was crispy on the outside and soft and moist in the inside. I made ours with no herbs or anything so we enjoyed it hot with butter and jam. Delicious!

As written, I think there’s too much water. I’m sure the right amount varies with humidity. Maryland summers call for less. I’d go with 1 1/3 cup water to start - certainly, not more than 1.5. I also added gluten to my all-purpose flour (3 tsp). Beautiful flavor and texture! I recommend you use 450 g of flour for the 3 cups.
I make this all the time. Prep it the night before and we have fresh bread in the morning. I love the crispy exterior.
